purpose: Bounded complete-section Translation inventory for cold calibration, repair, independent transfer and later edge checks without consuming protected true-exam material.

rules.exposure_downgrade: Any section exposed through reference review or repair cannot later serve as independent transfer evidence for the same mechanism.

tasks.context: A short passage on why planning requires more than predicting one exact future.

segments.text: Plans are often judged by whether their predictions turn out to be correct, but a useful plan may remain valuable even when the future differs from what was expected.
Its deeper function is to make assumptions visible, so that people can notice which changes would actually require them to act differently.
This is especially important when a decision must be made before all relevant information is available, as is usually the case outside controlled experiments.
A team that has identified the conditions under which its strategy should change is less likely to confuse persistence with discipline.
The goal, therefore, is not to eliminate uncertainty but to design decisions that can respond intelligently to it.

tasks.context: A passage on how metrics influence the behavior they are supposed to measure.

segments.text: Once a measure becomes important enough to affect rewards, people have a reason to improve the number even when doing so does not improve the underlying result.
This does not make measurement useless; rather, it means that a metric must be treated as evidence about performance instead of as performance itself.
The distinction is easy to state but difficult to preserve when organizations need a simple number on which to base repeated decisions.
What makes the problem harder is that the most visible distortions often appear only after people have learned how the system responds to their behavior.
For that reason, good measurement requires not only a clear metric but also periodic checks on whether the metric still tracks the outcome that originally justified it.

tasks.context: A passage on why mistakes become useful only when their causes can be reconstructed.

segments.text: An error does not automatically become a lesson merely because the person who made it later knows the correct answer.
To learn from failure, one must recover the decision as it appeared before the outcome was known, including the evidence that seemed persuasive at the time.
Otherwise, hindsight can make the mistaken choice look so obviously unreasonable that there is nothing left to explain.
The more accurately the original reasoning is reconstructed, the easier it becomes to distinguish a bad process from a reasonable process that happened to produce a bad result.
That distinction matters because correcting the wrong cause can make future decisions worse rather than better.

tasks.context: A passage on tools that reduce effort without replacing responsibility.

segments.text: Tools are most valuable when they reduce the cost of routine work without hiding the point at which human judgment is still required.
A system that produces a recommendation can save time, but the recommendation may be dangerous if users cannot tell what information it relied on or where its limits lie.
Transparency, in this sense, does not require every user to understand every technical detail.
It requires enough visibility for people to recognize when the tool is operating outside the conditions in which its output is trustworthy.
The aim is not to keep humans involved in every step, but to keep responsibility attached to the steps where error would materially change the decision.

tasks.context: A denser passage designed to test long attachment, qualification and degree/modality without being used as score-equivalent evidence.

segments.text: Institutions that appear resistant to change are sometimes preserving arrangements whose value is difficult to observe precisely because those arrangements prevent certain problems from becoming visible.
Removing a rule can therefore seem harmless at first, since the events it was designed to prevent may not occur immediately or may be attributed to unrelated causes.
This is not an argument for keeping every old rule, many of which survive long after their original purpose has disappeared.
It is an argument for asking what function a practice may be performing before concluding, from the absence of an obvious benefit, that it performs none.
Reform is strongest when it can distinguish between inherited friction that merely consumes effort and inherited constraints that quietly protect a valuable outcome.
